claims.text: Madhubani painting, also called Mithila art, is characterised by line drawings filled in with bright colours and contrasts or patterns.

quotes.quote: Madhubani painting, also referred to as Mithila Art (as it flourishes in the Mithila region of Bihar), is characterized by line drawings filled in by bright colours and contrasts or patterns.

claims.text: Madhubani painting is a ritual and decorative art practised primarily by women of the Madhubani region to make impermanent murals on mud walls.

quotes.quote: Also known as Mithila or Maithil painting, Madhubani painting is a ritual and decorative art form primarily practised by women of the Madhubani region to make impermanent murals on the mud walls.
This craft is mainly dominated by Women Community.

claims.text: The painting has traditionally been done by women of the region, though men have also become involved to meet market demand.

quotes.quote: This style of painting has been traditionally done by the women of the region, though today men are also involved to meet the demand.
Although the paintings are traditionally made by women, men are becoming more and more involved in order to meet market demand.

claims.text: Madhubani painting is done with fingers, twigs, brushes, nib-pens and matchsticks, using natural dyes and pigments, and is characterised by eye-catching geometric patterns.

quotes.quote: Madhubani Painting is done with fingers, twigs, brushes, nib-pens, and matchsticks, using natural dyes and pigments, and is characterized by eye-catching geometrical patterns.

claims.text: Traditionally painted on freshly plastered mud walls and floors of huts, Madhubani painting has moved to cloth, handmade paper and canvas.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, the painting was done on freshly plastered mud walls and floors of huts; but over the years it has moved to varied mediums including cloths, handmade papers, and canvas.
For commercial purposes, the work is now being done on paper, cloth, canvas etc.

claims.text: Floor and wall paintings, called aipanas and bhitti chitras, were traditionally painted to mark births, marriages and religious events, while the more elaborate kohabars were reserved for marriage ceremonies.

quotes.quote: Floor and wall paintings, known locally as aipanas and bhitti chitras respectively, were traditionally painted to mark occasions such as births, marriages and religious events, while the more elaborate paintings, called kohabars, were reserved for marriage ceremonies.

lede.text: Madhubani painting, also called Mithila art, is a ritual and decorative art of line drawings filled in with bright colours, practised primarily by women of the Madhubani region and traditionally made as impermanent murals on mud walls.
It developed in the Mithilanchal region of Bihar and received its Geographical Indication tag in 2007, and the GI application says it is mainly centred in the rural areas of Madhubani district.
Its traditional colours were mostly from natural sources; colours are applied flat with no shading, and gaps are generally filled with flowers, animals, birds and geometric designs.
After W. G. Archer noticed the murals in houses broken open by the 1934 earthquake, Pupul Jayakar's drought relief work encouraged the women to put their wall paintings on paper for sale.

sentences.text: W. G. Archer took the earliest academic notice of the painting in 1934, when an earthquake broke open the murals in Maithil households, and published 'Maithil Painting' in Marg in 1949.
Sources differ on Archer's post at the time: Neel Rekha and the GI application call him the SDO of Madhubani, and Szanton calls him the local Collector.
Archer's analysis centred on the paintings of Brahmanas and Kayasthas, which he called the two caste styles.

Sources say Pupul Jayakar sent the Bombay artist Bhaskar Kulkarni to encourage women to put their wall paintings on paper for sale, while a UMSAS account has the Bihar government fund him, and they differ on the drought's date, from 1960-61 to 1966-68.
Madhubani painting received official recognition in 1970, when the President of India gave an award to Jagdamba Devi of Jitwarpur.
Erika Moser spent four months in Jitwarpur in 1973, and sources differ on who began Godna painting, crediting Moser's persuasion of the Dusadh community, Harijan women, Shanti Devi or Shivan Paswan.
The Ethnic Arts Foundation, founded in 1980, set up the Mithila Art Institute, a free art school in Madhubani, in 2003.
Walls are plastered with cow dung or white-washed before painting, and on paper upper caste painters at times use a light brown cow dung wash to suggest a mud-plastered wall.
Traditional paintings use a minimal palette of pink, yellow, blue, red, parrot-green, black and white, mostly from natural sources processed by the artists themselves.
Paintings begin with a painted frame that mimics the wooden beams that framed the wall paintings.
Outlines are normally drawn as a double line, with the gap filled by cross or straight tiny lines.
Sources differ on sketching: some say paint goes on directly in a single flow with no preliminary sketch, while the GI application describes a sketch filled with colours.
According to the GI application, painters never rub off a wrong or crooked stroke, because they believe redoing a picture is inauspicious, and do whatever they paint in one go.
Brushes were made of bamboo splits or twigs, with cloth tied to a twig for bolder lines, and on paper painters use a holder and nib.
Godna painters draw paintings and outlines with minimal everyday resources such as gobar, kajal and bamboo sticks.
Black is prepared from soot, which village painters originally collected from the night lamp, and the IJTK study also names burnt barley seeds.
Yellow is made from turmeric, or from lime mixed with the milk of banyan leaves, red from kusum flowers and blue from indigo.
The district administration names wood apple leaves and the IJTK study bel leaves for green, and white is made from rice powder.
The district administration and UMSAS name palash flowers for orange, and the GI application names harshingara flowers.
The colours are mixed with goat milk or acacia gum, which UMSAS says increases their durability.
A 2020 study reports that painters' palettes are now filled with poster, acrylic and watercolours.
The colours are applied flat with no shading, and the decorative style abhors empty space, with gaps generally filled with flowers, animals, birds and geometric designs.
The most elaborate wall painting is done in the kohbar, the nuptial chamber, to bless the couple with fertility and protect them from the evil eye.
The kohabar's central motif is the purain, the lotus plant, surrounded by images such as parrots, fish, tortoise, the sun, the moon and a bamboo grove.
Bharni is marked by vivid colours and fewer lines, while kachni, or line painting, fills patterns with intricate line strokes made with fine-nibbed pens.
Godna paintings, crafted by Dalit Dusadh women, are mostly black and white, with themes of nature, the community's daily life and Dalit deities.
Tantrik paintings portray goddesses such as Kali, Durga and Lakshmi.
Techniques and images have often passed between artists and across castes at least since the paintings first went onto paper, and any group can now create any style.
The GI application says the painting is mainly centred in the rural areas of Madhubani district.
Ranti, Jitwarpur, Rasidpur and Rahika, all within 5 kilometres of the Madhubani district headquarters, are the four major centres of Mithila art.
The IJTK study says homes in villages of Darbhanga, Saharsa, Purnia and other districts also display paintings of ancient epics, fertility, love and religion.
UMSAS also names Simri among the special centres of painting, and a 2020 study interviewed artists in Simari village in Madhubani district.
Sources differ on which districts make up Mithila, and the region reaches into Nepal.
Madhubani was a subdivision of Darbhanga district from 1875 until 1972, when it became a separate district.
The Director of Industries, Bihar, filed GI application 37 on 22 August 2005, and the GI Registry issued certificate 31 on 16 May 2007.
The application was advertised as accepted in Geographical Indications Journal No. 14, dated 1 October 2006.
The registry lists the registration as valid up to 21 August 2025 and holds a renewal notice dated 26 November 2024.
The GI application, filed in 2005, states that 34% of the district's people are involved in Madhubani painting.
The district administration says the All India Handicrafts Board and the Government of India have been encouraging women artists to paint on handmade paper for commercial sale.
Madhubani painting has become a primary source of income for scores of families.

Szanton writes that since the late 1970s, aside from a brief flurry of commissions by Lalit Narayan Mishra, neither the Bihar nor national government has given the painting serious recognition or support.
